findings.notes: TOOL: computed by check_count_percent (MCP), which has no entry in this schema's technique enum; grim_percentage is its registered family and check_count_percent is documented as the strictly stronger sibling where the count is printed. The reproduction command names the actual verb. The paper's own numerator and denominator give 69.67%, not 70.00% -- a gap of 0.33 percentage points, and the printed value implies a denominator of ~4473 that appears nowhere in the paper. Two innocent explanations deserve weight: (1) compliance may have been computed as the MEAN of per-participant compliance rates rather than the pooled ratio, and those genuinely differ; (2) the authors may have rounded to a convenient figure. Against (2), the value is printed to two decimals, asserting four-significant-figure precision the pooled ratio does not support. I verified this is not an extraction or versioning artifact: the published XML prints '3131 out of 4494 ... (70.00%)' and the NIH author manuscript prints '3,131 out of 4,494 ... (70.00%)'. Both agree, so the discrepancy is the paper's. Note also 107 x 6 x 7 = 4494 exactly, so the denominator itself is internally correct.

findings.title: Table1 count percent all (Table 1, all gender, education and race/ethnicity rows)
findings.description: TOOL: check_table (MCP) dispatched check_count_percent on these cells; neither has a technique-enum entry, so the registered percentage family is named here and the reproduction command names the real verb. Denominator matters: 15 of 15 count/percent pairs that could be evaluated are consistent, to the last printed digit. Five cells printed as a bare '0' carry no percentage and were not evaluated. check_table also dispatched grim_percentage on the same cells; it correctly REFUSED all of them because a nominal/ordinal category label is not a GRIM-testable share, and those refusals are not evidence of anything.

findings.title: Table1 grim granularity (Table 1, BDI, CIA and DERS total-score rows)
findings.description: BDI 15.00 (10.00) is worth a reader's eye for a non-arithmetic reason: a mean of exactly 15.00 paired with an SD of exactly 10.00 is an unusually round combination. GRIMMER and SPRITE, which would test the SD, could not be run at all (see unchecked). findings.title: Table2 coefficients no df
findings.description: TOOL: check_regression_batch (MCP), the batched form of check_regression. This is a refusal, not an accusation: nothing was checked, so nothing is confirmed and nothing is impugned. It is nonetheless the single largest verification gap in the paper. Table 2 prints b, SE, p and a standardised beta for all 84 paths but no test statistic, no degrees of freedom and no confidence interval anywhere, and the level-1 sample size (the number of momentary eating-episode observations) is never reported. Compounding this, b and SE are printed to two decimals, so even with df the implied Wald ratio for a row such as -0.07 (0.03) spans roughly 1.86 to 3.00 and pins p only to a range of about .003 to .063

findings.title: Loc sd within stated range (Results, paragraph 1, LOC eating dimension descriptives)
findings.description: The bound here is the paper's own ('all ranges = 1-5'), not one I supplied, so this rests on a stated constraint. findings.title: Null claim m3 between ed loc
findings.description: The interval was DERIVED (b +/- 1.96 x SE on the normal scale, no df being available); the paper prints no confidence interval, so this is not the authors' own interval and its bounds inherit the two-decimal rounding of b and SE. The point is not that the paper made an arithmetic error but that 'not significant' is being read as 'no association': the data remain compatible with an effect as large as 1.79 on the same scale on which the paper's significant between-person effects are 0.82 to 1.00. No smallest effect size of interest is stated anywhere in the paper, so equivalence cannot be assessed and no conclusion of absence is licensed by these numbers alone.

findings.notes: A production/versioning defect, not an arithmetic anomaly, and not evidence against the authors. In the published XML the third row of each model's 'Direct effects' block reads 'Positive affect to Emotion dysregulation to LOC eating' -- a three-term mediation path sitting under 'Direct effects', whose label is verbatim identical to a different row in the same model's 'Indirect effects' block carrying different numbers. Three independent lines of evidence establish the intended label is 'Emotion dysregulation to LOC eating': (1) the NIH author manuscript prints exactly that for the same rows and the same numbers; (2) the Results narrative describes these very values as the emotion-dysregulation-to-LOC-eating direct effect -- 'within-person (beta = 0.13-0.14) and between-person (beta = 0.68-0.77)' matches Models 1 and 6 exactly; (3) Figure 1's path diagram specifies this path. I read the PDF label from the page's TEXT layer, not from its inferred grid, which pdfplumber flagged grid_unreliable because the page is rotated. Worth flagging to the publisher: a reader of the version of record alone cannot correctly identify what six rows of the paper's central table report.

findings.title: Statcheck no recomputable nhst (Body text, Results and Study Purpose sections)
findings.description: Zero statistics found is the correct result, not a tool failure, and it carries information: the paper contains no t(df), F(df1,df2), r(df), chi-squared(df) or z anywhere in its prose. Its inferential content is expressed entirely as bare p-values and standardised betas in Table 2. The consequence is that the most standard automated consistency check in this toolkit cannot touch this paper at all -- the same underlying reporting gap as table2_coefficients_no_df, seen from a second direction.

findings.notes: No tool computed this; it is a reading of Table 2 against the paper's own conclusions, so it is `manual` and capped at `suspicious`. The headline claim of 'notable variations ... based on the LOC eating dimension' is drawn by comparing significance verdicts across six separately estimated models, and at the between-person level the contrast rests on p = .048 versus p = .055 -- with the point estimate of the NON-significant coefficient (0.89) larger than that of the significant one (0.82). This is the classic error of treating the difference between significant and non-significant as itself significant. The paper never reports a test of whether any two LOC dimensions differ, and since the six outcomes come from the same participants at the same moments, such a test is both possible and the appropriate way to support the claim. The Discussion nonetheless builds a substantive theoretical account on the contrast ('there may be certain stages of a LOC eating episode that may be precipitated by such a sequence'). The innocent reading is that this reflects conventional practice in the field rather than anything unusual to this paper; the consequence is that the novelty claim is weaker than stated.
